summary: Defines the SIP History-Info header field, which records how and why a request reached a given application or user. This supports services such as voicemail and call distribution. It also defines related header parameters and a Privacy value to anonymize the information.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a package with stickers listing every place it was forwarded, so the final person knows how it got there.

questions: how to know why a sip call was redirected
what do rc mp and np mean in history-info
how does sip history-info privacy work
subtitle: A SIP header field that records every target a request was redirected to, so the receiver knows how and why it arrived.

tldr.problem: When a SIP request is retargeted, the original Request-URI is lost, yet services such as voicemail and call centers need to know how and why the request reached them.
tldr.mechanism: Each entity that forwards or retargets a request adds a History-Info entry holding the target URI, a dotted index that forms a tree, and an rc, mp or np tag saying how the target was chosen.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can rebuild the routing history, with a Privacy value of history to anonymize entries. This RFC obsoletes RFC 4244.

today: RFC 7044 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4244. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Request History Matters
sections.content:
SIP can already retarget a request, meaning a SIP entity changes the Request-URI and forwards it on. The trouble is that in the process, the old routing information can be forever lost. Many services need to know why and how a request arrived: calls to a call center from a click-to-talk link, call history and logging in call management software, and calls to voicemail servers.

RFC 7044 defines the History-Info header field to carry this retargeting history. It also defines the rc, mp and np parameters for the History-Info and Contact header fields, a history value for the Privacy header field, and a histinfo option tag. What an application does with the history is outside its scope.

The RFC also lists other uses: debugging, capturing aliases and GRUUs that a registrar or home proxy might overwrite, and preserving service-specific URIs that a downstream proxy could overwrite.
sections.plainLanguage: When a letter is forwarded from house to house, the last person only sees their own address. History-Info keeps a list of every address it passed through.

sections.title: The History-Info Header Field
sections.content:
Each hi-entry in the header describes one target used to forward the request. It has a mandatory hi-targeted-to-uri (the Request-URI as forwarded) and a mandatory index (the hi-index). It may also have one target tag, rc, mp or np, and extension parameters, which implementations that do not understand them MUST ignore.

The three tags say how the target was determined, and each carries the index of the entry whose URI was retargeted:

  • rc: the Request-URI changed but the target user stayed the same, for example when a user has several aliases.
  • mp: the request was mapped to a different user, so it names the 'mapped from' entry.
  • np: the Request-URI did not change, for example when a proxy just forwards to a next-hop proxy.

An entry can also hold a Reason header field (reflecting a response received for that target) and a Privacy header field, both placed in the headers component of the URI. Because of that, they are unavailable when the target is a Tel-URI. The header applies to out-of-dialog or initial dialog requests (such as INVITE, REGISTER, MESSAGE, REFER, OPTIONS, PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE) and their non-100 provisional or final responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sticker says where the package was sent, gets a number so the stickers stay in order, and can say whether it was the same person at a new address or a different person.

sections.title: How Each Role Handles It
sections.content:
A UAC MUST put the histinfo option tag in the Supported header field of an out-of-dialog or initial request if it wants History-Info in the response. For an initial request, the index starts at 1, and further forks get 2, 3 and so on.

Every SIP entity that receives a request MUST keep a cache of the hi-entries in the order received. If the Request-URI does not match the last entry's URI (the previous hop did not support History-Info), the entity adds an entry on that hop's behalf, with no rc, mp or np tag. When sending, it includes every cached entry plus one new entry for the outgoing request, in preorder of the tree. A Tel-URI SHOULD be turned into a SIP URI first.

When a response other than 100 arrives, or a request times out, the entity adds that entry to its cache and attaches a Reason header, such as the response code. A timeout is treated as a 408. It also adds any entries from the response that it lacks. Responses other than 100 MUST carry the cached entries, unless the request had no entries and no histinfo tag. A redirect server adds the right rc, mp or np parameter to each Contact in a 3xx response, and a proxy that retargets internally MUST add an entry for each internal target. A B2BUA may act as an intermediary and carry entries forward.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who passes the package along copies the old stickers onto the new box and adds one of their own. If a delivery fails, they write the reason next to that sticker.

sections.title: Index Numbers as a Tree
sections.content:
The hi-index is a series of nonnegative integers separated by dots, such as 1.1.2. Each dot is a forwarding hop, and the number after it is the order of the retarget at that hop. The result is a logical tree of the request's history, and entries are listed in preorder.

The rules in short: the first index is 1; forwarding without changing the target appends .1 (1.1 becomes 1.1.1); each further retarget by the same entity increments the last number (1.1.2); retargeting after a 3xx response increments the rightmost value (a request at 1.2 answered by a 302 yields 1.3); and forks, sequential or parallel, each get a unique, sequentially assigned index. If there is a gap because a hop did not add its entry, the next entity inserts an index of 0 first, so 1.1.2 becomes 1.1.2.0.1.

Gaps are not an error. Receivers MUST be ready for them, for example from intermediaries that do not support the header, or from outstanding parallel forks, and SHOULD tell applications about them. Duplicate indices are also possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers work like chapters and sub-chapters in a book. 1.2.1 means 'first thing that happened after the second step of the first stage', so you can see the whole branching story.

sections.title: Privacy and Reason Handling
sections.content:
The targets in History-Info can reveal information about the request's originator, so RFC 7044 adds the history priv-value to the Privacy header (RFC 3323). A UAC that sends any priv-value other than header MUST also include history. If it sends no priv-values, it MUST add history, but must not add critical. An intermediary can mark individual entries it wants protected by putting a Privacy header with the single value history in that entry's URI, and a UAS can do the same to hide the final target from the caller.

At a domain boundary, a Privacy Service anonymizes the affected entries rather than deleting them. It changes the URIs to use the domain anonymous.invalid and the user part anonymous, then removes the history value from the Privacy header.

The Reason header carries the SIP response code of the last response added to the cache, and any Reason headers in the response itself.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone wants their path kept secret, the boxes in the middle replace the real addresses with the word 'anonymous', but the stickers are still there so the order is not lost.

sections.title: How Applications Use It
sections.content:
Before using the data, an application MUST check for gaps. Because support for the header is optional, a service MUST define default behavior for requests with no or incomplete history, including entries from RFC 4244 entities that lack the new tags.

The RFC lists ways to pick useful entries. The entry referenced by the last rc tag in a request received by a UAS is the last AOR that was retargeted to a contact. The entry referenced by the first mp or rc tag gives a likely original target. Its non-normative examples are voicemail systems. A PBX voicemail finds the first entry tagged rc and uses the entry its index points to as the mailbox target. A consumer voicemail uses the last entry tagged rc. A call center might also show the agents the call was offered to before it reached the current one.

In the basic call example, Alice calls Bob at biloxi.example.com, and Bob's proxy forks to a PC and a phone. Bob can recover the original target by finding the last entry with an rc tag, which points to index 1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: A voicemail box reads the stickers to find out whose mailbox the call was really meant for, so it plays the right greeting.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility
sections.content:
Using TLS (RFC 5246) is strongly RECOMMENDED for confidentiality. Without it, the intermediary MUST make sure messages stay in a secured environment or inside its domain. That puts History-Info at about the same security level as other SIP headers added by intermediaries. Using the SIPS scheme protects against outside tampering, but every intermediary on the path is trusted, and a malicious one could delete or rewrite entries. The RFC does not try to prevent or detect that.

Appendix A lists requirements, including that the receiver be able to detect altered content, that ordering be preserved, that the provider be authenticated, and that only entities processing the request see the information.

Compared with RFC 4244, this document adds the rc, mp and np parameters, the index of 0 for gaps, and anonymizing instead of removing entries. It also drops the mandate for TLS on every hop and strengthens several SHOULDs to MUSTs, such as the UAC including the option tag. It states that these changes do not cause compatibility problems, since older implementations ignore the new parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The stickers are only as trustworthy as everyone who handled the package. Locking the delivery truck (TLS) helps against outsiders, but not against a dishonest courier.

items.label: Same user, new Request-URI
items.desc: Target user is retained, for example an alias or a registered contact.

items.label: Mapped to another user
items.desc: Target is a user other than the one for the retargeted Request-URI.

items.label: No change
items.desc: Request-URI is unchanged, such as a plain next-hop forward.
